Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

vignette:
Elena was thirty-nine years old, a city council member in a mid-sized Midwestern town, and she was exhausted. She came to therapy at her husband's quiet but persistent urging, after months of him finding her standing in the dark of their bedroom at three in the morning, staring at the door. She would say she was just listening. What she meant was that she was waiting for the sound of something breaking.

The event she could not fully remember was from when she was seven years old. She had been standing in the upstairs hallway of her childhood home, in her pajamas, holding the banister. Her father had come home late. Her mother had said something. Then there was shouting, a crash, a sound like a piece of furniture being shoved across the floor, and then her mother's voice went quiet. Elena remembered the way the wooden banister felt under her small hand-smooth and cool, with a small knot in the wood that pressed into her palm. She remembered the smell of dust and floor wax. But she could not remember what happened next. She could not remember who called the police, or how she got back to her room, or what her father said the next morning. Those parts of the night were simply gone, like pages torn from a book. What remained were fragments: the sound of glass breaking, the blue light of the television still on in the living room, and the feeling of her own body frozen in place, one hand on the banister, bare feet on the cold floor. Even now, when a memory surfaced-usually triggered by something she could not predict, like the clatter of a dropped plate in a restaurant or the sudden slam of a car door-she would feel that same stillness lock her body. Her shoulders would square, her knees would lock, her hand would curl as if gripping that banister again. She would be back in that hallway, waiting.

As an adult, Elena had built a life that seemed stable: a husband she trusted, a career in public service, a house with a yard. But inside that life, her world had narrowed to a handful of safe places. Her home was one, but only if she was alone. If her husband came home unexpectedly early, she felt a spike of alarm before she could stop it. Her office at city hall was another, but only when the door was closed and she could see the hallway through the window. She had come to believe that danger was always nearby, that it could come from anyone, that the only way to stay safe was to watch. She watched people constantly-at council meetings, at the grocery store, at stoplights. She studied their hands, their faces, the way they stood. She was looking for the shift, the flicker of anger, the tightening of a jaw that would mean something was about to happen. Her colleagues thought she was intensely focused. They did not know she was scanning for threat.

The cost of this vigilance had accumulated slowly. She had stopped attending community events that involved large crowds, citing scheduling conflicts. She had stopped walking to the coffee shop two blocks from her office because the door there swung open too fast and too loudly. She had begun to have trouble sleeping: she would lie awake for hours, her mind circling the same blank spaces in her memory, trying to fill them in, trying to understand what she had seen that she could not now retrieve. Her husband had started sleeping in the guest room because she would flinch when he turned over in bed.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was a moment at a town hall meeting two weeks ago. A man in the audience had raised his voice, frustrated about a zoning issue, and for a split second Elena had felt her body lock into that childhood freeze-hand on the banister, feet on the cold floor-right there at the dais, in front of sixty people. She had managed to keep her face neutral, but afterward she had sat in her car for twenty minutes, shaking. She was terrified that next time she would not be able to hide it. She came to therapy hoping to stop the watching, to sleep through the night, and to understand what had happened in that hallway-but she was also afraid that remembering the rest of it would be worse than not knowing.
